doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Messenger jobs, Milt Hinton's respect, other musicians' day jobs
summary: He tells of Milt Hinton seeing him deliver papers and Mona Hinton's later words, and lists musicians like McCoy Tyner and Bob Cranshaw with day jobs.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: After taxes. And this was before the bikes came in. I was a messenger. I was taking the subway and walking. Package was fifty cents then. Then my big job came after that, I worked with the Wall Street Journal I had two bags of newspapers. I’d get there at six o’clock in the morning and pack up my bags and so I was walking one day, I had two bags and I was going to the Pan Am building. And that was my last drop off. So that’s why I love going there because I could just drop three hundred papers. So I’m walking around and I see the Judge, Milt Hinton, pushing his upright bass with his electric bass. Because you know during that time Milt Hinton and Richard Davis and all those people, they were on first call. George Duvivier. So he was shocked, he said “Judge, what are you doing?” I said, “Well Judge, I’m trying to take care of my family.” So he didn’t say well give me your number I’ve got something for you. He said, “Well a man’s got to do what a man’s got to do.” And I didn’t take it — I kept stepping. And then I kind of quit that job and started doing some other things. But then, before he passed, his lovely wife Mona, rest her soul, she told me she said, “You know I want to tell you something, that Milton always respected you.” Because Milt Hinton went to the same high school my wife went to, Wendell Phillips, Nat Cole went there and Ruth Jones. Ruth Jones is down in Washington. She went there to Wendell Phillips. My wife went there, Lou Rawls, Sam Cooke, they all went to Wendell Phillips High School. But she told me, Mona Hinton, she said, “You know Milton always respected you and loved your playing,” and she said he told her that when he saw you that day delivering [inaudible] he gained more respect.” I said, “Well I appreciate it but I’m just doing what I have to do, I don’t deserve no brownie points for that.” So that’s how that happened. So then a lot of musicians, I think McCoy Tyner drove a cab for a while and a lot of musicians — Ahmad Jamal had a day job even though he was working in Chicago. He was talking about it. Ahmad Jamal he worked with [inaudible] Scott, Izzy Carlson was a mailman. Izzy Carlson would come in in the morning and we had breakfast parties and play with us and Frank Strozier, and go finish his route. Vernell Fournier had a job at Chills. Ernie [inaudible] worked at the post office. Bob Cranshaw was a sanitation man. Hello? And I mean he wouldn’t mind my saying it because it’s the truth, that’s right. So everybody had some kind of day job but the difference was they had a day job but they still had a music job at night. Me, I had to resort too because I didn’t have a music job but whenever I took a day job then the music gigs would come in so to speak.
